newsitem.title: USA: Gephardt budget move a declaration of independence.
newsitem.headline: Gephardt budget move a declaration of independence.

text.p: House Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt's decision Tuesday to fight a balanced budget deal moved him further from the White House and closer to his party's liberal wing for a possible presidential bid.

Gephardt's opposition is not expected to derail the budget pact negotiated by President Clinton and congressional Republicans. Congress is likely to approve the budget outlines this week with the support of a majority of Democrats.
But by going against the tide, the Missouri Democrat has asserted his independence from Clinton and Vice President Al Gore -- a probable contender for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2000.
Gephardt is also strengthening already close ties to organized labor. The AFL-CIO, one of the Democratic Party's biggest donors, opposes the budget plan.

Using populist themes he has long sounded, Gephardt argued that the pact abandoned core Democratic values. He charged that programs for the middle class and poor were being cut to finance a unwarranted tax cut for the wealthy.
He flatly denied his decision was political.

"I have one thing on my mind, and one thing on my mind only, and that is the people I represent," Gephardt said on the House floor. "This is not politics. This is not some election. This is about the future of the country."

Gephardt is expected to distance himself from the White House again next week when he gives a speech in Detroit on trade with China. Clinton wants to renew the country's preferential trading status. Gephardt opposes renewal.
White House officials said the senator told the president at a Tuesday meeting he hoped his motives would not be questioned.

Asked if Gephardt was positioning himself to challenge him for the presidency, Gore told reporters: "Oh, I have no idea about anything like that. These are important issues that are deserving of full discussion and debate, and I respect differing opinions."
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton would work closely with Gephardt. "Let's not run the 2000 campaign in 1997. Let's wait two or three years," he said.

The budget deal is designed to eliminate the deficit over five years. It includes about $130 billion in Medicare and Medicaid cuts and a net $85 billion tax cut, including trims in estate and capital gains taxes.
Gephardt said the tax cuts could balloon in later years, increasing the deficit. He charged that the plan fell short in the fields of education, transportation and children's health.
But his opposition carries political risks. Gephardt is betting the plan will prove unpopular with voters at a time when opinion polls show a majority of Americans support the agreement.

It also opens a rift in the Democratic leadership. Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle is a booster of the budget deal. House Democratic Whip David Bonior, who has fought Republicans on a host of issues, will support the budget measure.
"The fights are down the road," Bonior, a Michigan Democrat, said. He will seek changes when Congress passes tax and spending bills needed to implement the budget deal.

Conservative Democrats too embraced the proposal. Texas Democratic Rep. Charlie Stenholm called the budget fight "a fundamental fight within the structure of the Democratic party." "The Democratic Party didn't get into the minority by accident," he said. "We worked at it and now we've got to change it."
This is not Gephardt's first split with the White House.

He voted last year against a Republican welfare bill signed by Clinton, and he has been at odds with the president not only on China trade but on Clinton's desire to extend a free trade agreement to South American nations.

"He's positioning himself excellently to command the liberal base of the party in the primaries. From his point of view it was an excellent decision," House Republican Leader Dick Armey of Texas said.
